key_insight: A multimodal wearable assessment could reduce Parkinson’s motor testing to a smaller set of upper-limb tasks while preserving strong discrimination between patients and controls.
clinical_relevance: The approach points toward shorter, clinically anchored digital motor assessments that may be easier to deploy and standardize, but it still needs independent validation before use in care.
method: 31 people with Parkinson’s disease and 30 matched controls completed seven standardized MDS-UPDRS III tasks.
Surface EMG and full-body inertial motion capture were combined with musculoskeletal simulations.
A leakage-free machine-learning pipeline with cross-validation, permutation testing, task fusion, and stability-based biomarker selection was used.
evidence_signal: Pronating-supination was the top-performing task (ROC-AUC 0.94), and multimodal fusion across four upper-limb tasks maintained high discrimination (ROC-AUC 0.93; balanced accuracy 0.92).
watch_item: The sample was modest and from a specific disease-stage range, so generalizability and real-world robustness remain uncertain.
paper_title: A Reduced Digital Motor Assessment using Multimodal Biomarkers in Parkinson's Disease
